video.title: The Real Reason We Should Revive Extinct Animals

protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Lemonfox transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Story: cloning an extinct animal needs a whole living cell (nucleus swapped into an egg); by 2000 one bucardo was left, biologists froze its tissue, and in 2003 a cloned baby bucardo was born -- with a malformed lung, and it didn't survive (226.3). Opening on the Jurassic Park mosquito line (144.7) is a stronger hook but runs ~82s; both edges work.

Hot take: people online pointed out the 'dire wolves' are really genetically modified gray wolves -- but that was intentional; the project's scientist wants the fewest edits possible because every change risks something unpredicted and he wants healthy animals (386.3). Continuing to 'they're trying to de-extinct what the animal did' (410.0) also works; say both. Opens past 'In fact,'. Speaker change to the scientist at 367.0 inferred from text.

Claim with a turn: five mass extinctions in Earth's history and many scientists say we're in a sixth, caused by us, which hits our food and homes -- but the same tools built to bring back extinct animals can keep animals from going extinct (539.9); naming it 'genetic rescue' (546.2) is acceptable. Starts right after the sponsor read.

Surprising fact and fix: every black-footed ferret alive today is a first cousin; the population nearly vanished in 1979 and now has a tiny gene pool (bottleneck), so scientists sequence DNA from a hundred-year-old museum specimen and edit it into living ferrets.

Explanation: the northern quoll may be extinct in the wild within ten years because it eats toxic invasive cane toads, and a single letter of genetic code decides whether it dies or is resistant -- introduce that one change and save a species (650.1). 'There are projects to do this on coral reefs' (661.4) is an acceptable longer end.

Question and answer: why de-extinct at all? Killing the Tasmanian tiger removed Tasmania's only apex predator -- wallabies and kangaroos exploded, shrubs and birds suffered, Tasmanian devils spread a face cancer predators used to cull -- a butterfly effect, so some say the only way to rebalance the ecosystem is to put the tiger back (721.2).

What happens when you drop a predator back into an environment after a century? Researchers took replica thylacines into the bush: the prey animals ignore a fox or a goat, but see a thylacine and 'they are out of it' (805.5). Speaker switches to a researcher at ~781.8, inferred from text.

Debate: would a revived thylacine know how to be a predator? One expert doubts it'll ever be in the wild; advocates say behaviour is hardwired -- house cats fed biscuits for generations still pounce the moment a mouse runs by (846.3). 'We don't really know until we try, and they're trying' (849.4) is an acceptable end. Multiple speakers inferred from text.

Closing take: the most optimistic part isn't bringing back animals from the past but using this science to keep today's animals healthy -- 'de-extinction science is conservation science'; the real debate isn't what's a dire wolf, it's what responsibility we have to the world we created (940.8).

also_ok.why: 'Imagine you're a mad scientist ... here's the recipe': breed close living relatives back toward the extinct animal, as with the quagga zebra, hunted out by 1883 and already brought back in a version. Leaves the 'three paths' framing open and shows a toy on screen.

negatives.why: Cold open: 1933 footage of the last Tasmanian tiger ('look at this') and a tease that the real story is something else -- screen narration plus a promise.
'A distraction from the real huge-if-true use ... but first, let me show you something' into the phone-case sponsor read.
'They're following the recipe', 'this is the closest living animal', 99.9% identical, 'wait, 0.1 percent?' -- leans on the recipe framing and an on-screen animal.
'Did we not learn our lesson from Jurassic Park?' -- a string of questions with no answer in the stretch.
